content: In each country, programs may encounter a high proportion of cases with Grade 2 Disabilities (G2D) in regions where the healthcare system is underdeveloped and access to medical services is limited. The quality of care, as reflected in metrics such as treatment completion rates, can be used to prioritize and target interventions in specific areas, regions, districts, or sub-districts. The relevance of key intervention areas will vary depending on the epidemiological context, and this will be detailed in the corresponding sections of these guidelines. For example, in areas with a high number of individuals living with leprosy-related disabilities, there will be a greater need for services focused on disability management. Analyzing hard-to-reach areas and identifying vulnerable groups, such as migrants, can guide national planning efforts. Cultural and geographical challenges may necessitate specific approaches, such as active screening campaigns, to ensure that leprosy patients are identified and treated. This baseline analysis of epidemiological data compared to available services will serve as the foundation for each country. State or regional managers will determine which actions are most relevant among those outlined under the three pillars of the strategy. Partners and stakeholders are encouraged to support countries in conducting this analysis as a first step toward preparing national operational plans and securing funding. Actions designed to achieve global or regional impact are proposed as global and regional actions in subsequent sections of this manual. The goal of the Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 is to reduce the burden of leprosy by 2020. However, the burden of leprosy can be understood from at least two perspectives. The most relevant epidemiological measure of the burden is the number of new cases detected, defined as the number of individuals diagnosed with leprosy during a specific time period, usually one year, within a given population. Since the incidence of leprosy is difficult to measure, the new case detection rate is used as a proxy indicator for incidence. Globally, the case detection rate, expressed as the notification rate per 100,000 population, appears to be declining slowly. However, in many areas, it remains static, and in some places, it is even increasing. Changes in detection rates occur gradually over decades due to the long incubation period of the disease. These changes are influenced by factors such as Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination coverage, socioeconomic development, and effective leprosy program practices, particularly early diagnosis. New cases will continue to emerge for many years from the pool of already infected individuals who are in the incubation phase. Therefore, diagnostic and treatment services, as well as disability prevention and rehabilitation services, must be maintained. The burden of leprosy can also be measured as the prevalence of the disease, defined as the number of individuals undergoing treatment at a specific point in time (point prevalence). Registered prevalence is significantly influenced by the number of new cases diagnosed and treated, as well as the duration of treatment. From the perspective of individuals affected by leprosy, particularly those with disabilities, the burden includes the social rejection and stigma they may face. Leprosy can result in disabilities affecting the hands, feet, and eyes, and in some cases, blindness. It is estimated that over 3 million people are living with disabilities caused by leprosy, many of which could have been prevented. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 emphasizes the need to reduce this burden by increasing efforts to detect new cases early, thereby preventing disabilities, and by improving the management of acute and chronic complications caused by leprosy reactions. This includes promoting self-care support activities, rehabilitation, and reconstructive surgery. In addition to physical consequences, leprosy often causes significant psychological and social suffering, which is another aspect of the burden. This suffering is frequently a result of stigma and discrimination. The Operational Manual advocates for a person-centered, holistic approach that addresses the social and psychological challenges faced by each affected individual. It also provides examples of activities that can be implemented to combat stigma and discrimination wherever they exist. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020 highlights the importance of providing high-quality leprosy services as an essential component of an effective health program. Quality is achieved through appropriate training of staff at all levels, regular technical supervision, and the capacity to report and monitor key indicators. Ensuring quality requires the willingness of staff to improve their skills and the functioning of the health services in which they work. High-quality leprosy services should be accessible to all individuals in need of diagnosis and treatment, without barriers related to geography, economics, or gender. They should promptly identify and manage reactions and other complications, be patient-centered, and respect patients' rights, including the right to timely and appropriate treatment, privacy, and confidentiality. The healthcare system must be flexible to meet patients' needs and capable of providing accompanied multidrug therapy (A-MDT) when necessary to facilitate adherence. It should empower patients and their families by disseminating information about the disease, its consequences, the patient's role in care, and the available services, including rehabilitation. Patients and their families should be informed about the disease, treatment options, possible reactions, and rehabilitation services, with an emphasis on the importance of contact examination. Case management should address all aspects based on solid scientific evidence, including timely and accurate diagnosis with supportive counseling, free and user-friendly treatment with multidrug therapy (MDT), appropriate and timely disability prevention interventions, and the provision of services for complications and rehabilitation, including reconstructive surgery, as needed. Patients and their families should have access to psychological and socioeconomic support to ensure treatment adherence and facilitate social inclusion. Cured patients and their families should be considered valuable resources for the health system. Effective leprosy control requires an integrated approach that ensures equity, accessibility, cost-effectiveness, and long-term sustainability. Leprosy elimination activities should be implemented through general health services, including integrated referral facilities. Integration not only improves access to treatment but also reduces stigma and discrimination faced by individuals affected by leprosy. In defining the needs of leprosy programs, the context of integration should not be overlooked. Integration means that day-to-day patient management, as well as recording and reporting, become the responsibility of general health staff. However, specialized services must still be guaranteed within an integrated system. For example, general medical officers with additional training in leprosy, dermatologists, or surgeons should be available, and specialists should refer patients back to peripheral health facilities for continued treatment. Specialized referral services for leprosy should be part of the general health services, similar to how a surgeon in a district hospital is part of the general health services. Peripheral general health workers in endemic areas should be capable of diagnosing and treating uncomplicated leprosy cases, which represent the majority of cases, and should know where to find specialized health services. All peripheral health staff should be aware of the clinics and health staff to whom they can refer patients to minimize difficulties for patients. A directory of specialized services and sites should be available. Staff at all levels should be able to seek specialized advice through telemedicine or centers of excellence to ensure patients receive the necessary care. Good communication between peripheral and referral center healthcare workers should be maintained to discuss patients' progress and provide opportunities for further training. Mobile phones and text messaging can facilitate timely communication. Urgent referral is required for severe reactions, such as reversal reactions involving major nerve trunks, neuritis (including silent neuritis), erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) reactions, severe infections of the hand or foot, and eye involvement in leprosy. Specific eye problems requiring urgent referral include recent loss of visual acuity, painful red eye, recent inability to close the eye (lagophthalmos), and reactions in facial skin patches. Other cases requiring urgent referral include severe adverse drug reactions or discharging ulcers/burns. Peripheral healthcare workers may also need to refer patients to confirm uncertain diagnoses, as early treatment is crucial to stop transmission and prevent complications. In areas where leprosy is less common, the ability to suspect leprosy and refer patients to a referral unit is the most important skill for peripheral general health workers. Diagnosis confirmation should be done at specialized referral centers, which must also have the capacity to initiate treatment and provide initial follow-up. Proper referral back and forth is essential to avoid losing track of leprosy suspects and cases. Continuation of treatment can be delegated to the peripheral health facility serving the patient's community after adequate orientation by the referral center on possible side effects and timely identification of reactions. Referral centers will manage difficult complications of leprosy, and rehabilitative surgical services will be even more centralized. Some referral services may also be provided through mobile units. Community-based organizations (CBOs), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and private institutions play a crucial role in providing leprosy services close to the community. Networking with these institutions, along with referral centers, medical colleges, and dermatologists, is key to ensuring comprehensive, patient-tailored care. These non-governmental institutions can serve as effective focal centers for both basic and specialized services and interventions. Their activities can be well-coordinated within national programs, saving resources while ensuring service provision. It is important to develop linkages with other sectors, both public and private, and within the community, including organizations and self-help groups of individuals affected by leprosy, to facilitate access to care and ensure high-quality leprosy services. For countries with a relatively high burden of the disease, national coalitions of stakeholders contributing to leprosy services can help raise funds, increase awareness, and create demand for quality services. In some countries, leprosy programs are still managed through a vertical structure, either independently or within joint tuberculosis/leprosy programs or under Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTD) programs. These programs typically have administrative/managerial focal points at various levels of the health services, while primary healthcare networks provide integrated services for communicable and non-communicable diseases. Coordination between levels of care must ensure proper management of MDT and ancillary drugs, refresher training, supportive supervision of field workers, enhanced quality of referral services, and monitoring of quality data to assess program progress. In areas lacking resources, at least one central-level unit should be responsible for leprosy control, ensuring the capacity to detect, treat, and report leprosy accurately in at least one center in the country and facilitating access to care for all cases. Ultimately, the responsibility for controlling and eliminating leprosy lies with the national authorities of each country. Partners and stakeholders can play a supportive role in sustaining and enhancing political commitment. Following the declaration of leprosy elimination, many countries have experienced reduced resources for leprosy activities. This lack of funding may have contributed to late detection, resulting in an increasing rate of patients already disabled at the time of diagnosis. Delays are also attributed to the loss of expertise and the lack of structured involvement of the private sector, including private-for-profit and informal private sectors, which are particularly important in Asia and Africa. The Bangkok Declaration, signed in 2013 by health ministers of high-burden countries with the support of The Nippon Foundation, has somewhat renewed momentum. However, as leprosy becomes a rare disease and other communicable and non-communicable disease programs compete for priority, addressing leprosy becomes increasingly challenging. Expanding partnerships beyond traditional leprosy-focused organizations to include those involved in disabilities and social development may offer new opportunities. Even within traditional partnerships, innovative approaches are needed to sustain progress.
